query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer during exposure above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation behavior of the X element. When X is Al, its preferential oxidation produces a continuous, slow-growing, dense alumina (α-Al2O3) scale with low lattice mismatch and low oxygen diffusivity, which suppresses further oxidation and minimizes stress-driven cracking or spallation. In contrast, when X is Mn or Si—or when no such active element is present—the resulting oxides are less ordered, grow more rapidly, and are prone to stress accumulation, leading to unstable, cracking, or spalled oxide scales compared to the Al-containing alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloys synthesized with systematic variations: one with X = Al, another with X = Mn, a third with X = Si, and a baseline alloy with negligible X addition.
generation.intervention: Prepare alloy variants with controlled compositions (varying the X element) and conduct isothermal oxidation tests at 900 °C for up to 50 hours in a well-controlled oxidative (air or oxygen-rich) atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Oxidation testing at 900 °C for 40–50 hours in a controlled, high-oxygen partial pressure environment; samples must have equivalent processing histories to ensure comparable single-phase microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an Al-enriched sub-oxide layer (α-Al2O3) at the metal–oxide interface that establishes a coherent, graded diffusion barrier, in contrast to the disordered, rapidly growing oxides produced when Mn or Si is the dominant active element.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the active element governs oxide stability: Al, due to its favorable thermodynamics and slower diffusion kinetics, forms a thin, adherent, protective alumina scale that kinetically limits further oxygen ingress and minimizes interfacial stress. In contrast, Mn and Si form oxides that either grow too rapidly or have higher lattice mismatches, producing unstable oxide layers that crack or spall under thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy containing Al will form a stable, uniformly adherent, and mechanically coherent oxide layer that persists during high-temperature exposure, whereas alloys with Mn, Si, or without a significant active element will exhibit non-uniform oxide growth with evidence of cracking, spallation, or rapid oxidation kinetics.
generation.baseline: The baseline alloy is the CrFeCoNi alloy without any significant X (Al, Mn, or Si) addition, used to compare the effect of adding an active element on the oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to single-phase CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys exposed to oxidative or corrosive environments at temperatures above 900 °C for durations up to 50 hours.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the possible influence of minor variations in microstructure or elemental segregation that could affect the oxidation kinetics independently of the X element. Additionally, external factors such as trace impurities or slight differences in processing conditions may alter the scale adhesion properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform isothermal oxidation tests on the four alloy variants (X = Al, Mn, Si, and baseline with no significant X) at 900 °C for 50 hours. Characterize the oxide scales using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to assess scale morphology, phase composition, and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness via cross-sectional imaging
Phase identification and crystal structure of the oxides (XRD)
Elemental depth profiles at the metal–oxide interface (EDS)
Adhesion strength tests (e.g., scratch test or indentation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly more coherent, adherent, and continuous oxide layer compared to the Mn or Si alloy variants and the baseline—or if the differences in oxide stability are not statistically significant—the hypothesis that selective oxidation of Al governs the formation of a protective oxide scale is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As no Cr-rich oxide of the form Cr2O3 formed during the oxidation test to work as a barrier and inhibit or slow down the diffusion of Mn element, no protection of the substrate beneath the scale to further oxidation was thus available [].

It is worth mentioning that all the prior studies on microstructural refinement and the oxidation behavior of the resulting materials were limited to conventional structural materials only. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, there has been no study on achieving remarkable oxidation resistance in HEAs through microstructural refinement. In the current work, microstructural refinement of the AlCoCrFeNi HEA was accomplished via severe surface deformation using stationary friction processing (SFP). The processing resulted in ultrafine-grain structure with a significant fraction of nanograins in the as-cast HEA along with significant elemental homogenization. The processed HEA samples demonstrated exceptional oxidation resistance, and the reported mass gain values are among the lowest for the investigated HEA. The remarkable performance of the processed HEAs was attributed to the formation of an intact, dense, uniformly distributed oxide scale, favored by large grain boundary density, higher surface free energy, and uniform elemental distribution.

proposals.intervention: Systematically vary the X element by comparing alloys with X = Al versus X = Mn or Si, including a baseline alloy with no significant X addition.
proposals.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests at 900 °C for up to 50 hours in a controlled oxidative atmosphere (e.g., air or O2-rich environment).
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of a coherent, continuous, Al-enriched sub-oxide (α-Al2O3) layer at the metal–oxide interface.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that the selective oxidation of Al produces a dense, slow-growing alumina scale with low lattice mismatch and excellent adhesion, which limits oxygen inward diffusion and minimizes volumetric stress. In contrast, Mn or Si produce oxides that are less dense or prone to stress accumulation, leading to crack initiation and spallation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al will display a stable, coherent oxide that persists under the high-temperature exposure, while those with X = Mn or Si (or the baseline without X) develop unstable, cracking or spalling oxide scales under identical conditions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests whether the nature of X governs oxide stability via its intrinsic oxidation kinetics and resulting oxide properties. The comparison against a baseline (no X addition) provides a direct measure of the effect of the X element in promoting a protective oxide scale.

proposals.material_system: CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloy prepared in single-phase versus multiphase states
proposals.intervention: Tailor the processing route to produce either a homogeneous single-phase (via rapid solidification) or a multiphase (via conventional casting/annealing) alloy, with the Mn addition kept constant.
proposals.conditions: Expose both microstructural variants to 900 °C in an oxidative (air) environment for similar durations (e.g., 40–50 hours).
proposals.structural_mediator: Uniform vs. heterogeneous elemental distribution influencing oxide nucleation; in the single-phase state, a homogeneous Mn depletion zone facilitates a consistent oxide scale, whereas locally segregated phases in the multiphase alloy lead to differential oxidation behaviour.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that a uniform, single-phase microstructure promotes a coherent, adherent oxide by minimizing local variations in oxidation-induced volume changes. In contrast, multiphase materials suffer from mismatched oxidation kinetics among constituent phases, resulting in non-uniform oxide growth, internal stresses, and eventual spallation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The single-phase HEA will form a stable, crack‐free oxide layer, while the multiphase alloy will exhibit localized cracking and oxide spallation due to internal stress concentrations at phase boundaries.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By controlling the microstructural state, this approach isolates the role of phase homogeneity on the formation and persistence of protective oxides, directly testing whether uniform elemental distribution promotes oxide coherence.

proposals.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to the alloy to form an initial thin, coherent Si-rich oxide layer before high-temperature exposure.
proposals.conditions: First, pre-treat the alloy at 700 °C for 10 hours in a mildly oxidative atmosphere (low oxygen partial pressure), and then subject the sample to 900 °C in a fully oxidative or corrosive environment for prolonged durations.
proposals.structural_mediator: A pre-formed, continuous SiO2-based interfacial oxide layer that acts as a nucleation barrier for further oxidation and limits abrupt growth stresses.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that the pre-oxidation step provides a templated, stable oxide layer that adapts to the alloy’s lattice parameters. This layer minimizes the nucleation of later, unstable oxide phases by limiting abrupt oxygen uptake and reducing interfacial stresses, thereby ensuring long-term scale coherence during later high-temperature exposure.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Pre-treated CrFeCoNiSi samples will maintain a coherent, adherent oxide scale with low spallation rates compared to untreated counterparts, which are expected to exhibit rapid formation of unstable oxides that crack or delaminate.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction tests whether a pre-established oxide layer can govern subsequent oxidation kinetics and mechanical integrity at the metal–oxide interface, offering a controlled comparison against untreated samples.

proposals.material_system: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy (X = Al or Mn) with a modified near-surface composition
proposals.intervention: Perform ion implantation on the alloy surface to induce a near-surface enrichment of the active X element (e.g., Al) prior to high-temperature oxidation testing.
proposals.conditions: Subject the ion-implanted samples to 900 °C for 40–50 hours in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, ensuring that the implantation depth is on the order of tens to a few hundred nanometers.
proposals.structural_mediator: Creation of a compositional gradient in the near-surface region that promotes the formation of a tailored, diffusion-resistant oxide scale with graded composition and reduced interfacial stresses.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that ion implantation produces a chemically modified surface layer that preferentially forms a protective oxide (e.g., alumina when Al-enriched) via enhanced local oxidation of the implanted species. This gradient suppresses rapid oxygen ingress and minimizes abrupt phase changes at the oxide/metal interface, thus reducing stress-induced cracking and spallation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The ion-implanted alloys will develop a uniformly adherent, coherent oxide layer that remains stable under high-temperature exposure, whereas non-implanted (baseline) samples will display less controlled oxidation with increased spallation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach leverages surface engineering to directly control the oxidation behaviour at the metal interface, providing a clear testable mechanism for oxide stability based on near-surface composition modification.

decision.rationale: Direction C directly tests the role of the X element by comparing alloys with Al versus Mn or Si (and a baseline with no active X addition) to determine if selective oxidation of Al leads to a thermodynamically stable and mechanically coherent alumina scale. This approach cleanly targets the mechanistic question of what governs oxide stability—specifically, the intrinsic oxidation kinetics and resulting oxide properties of the X element. The abundant supporting evidence on alumina scale formation and its protective characteristics, along with well‐defined test conditions (900 °C, controlled oxidative atmosphere, and a defined baseline alloy), underpins choosing this direction.
